title: Successful Management of Biliary Ascariasis in a High-Endemic Zone and Low-Resource Setting in Ethiopia
case_text:
A 35-year-old woman presented to our hospital, Dilla University Referral Hospital, located in Dilla, southern Ethiopia, with abdominal pain of one-day duration. The pain was in the right upper abdomen, intermittent, colicky, and nonradiating, with no aggravating or relieving factors, and accompanied by anorexia and nausea. She denied any history of fever or vomiting. On physical examination, her vitals were normal, and icteric sclera was noted. Her abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the right hypochondriac region. Her laboratory investigations (Table 1) revealed neutrophilic leucocytosis, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and elevated alanine transaminase. On stool examination, ova of Ascaris lumbricoides were seen. Furthermore, ultrasonography (USG) of the abdomen revealed worms in the distal common bile duct with partial obstruction, a dilated gallbladder, and dilated right and left hepatic ducts (Figures 1 and 2).
Based on the high endemicity of ascariasis that is limited to the gastrointestinal tract in Ethiopia, the patients' history, clinical evaluation, stool examination, and USG report, a diagnosis of obstructive jaundice secondary to biliary ascariasis was made. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first case report in Ethiopia about biliary ascariasis, although it is quite common to see ascariasis cause disease manifestations limited to the small and large bowel. The management was done by administering intravenous normal saline, intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g bid, intravenous metronidazole 500 mg bid, intravenous hyoscine butyl bromide, and a single dose of 200 mg oral albendazole. A follow-up USG after 2 days did not reveal any worm in the common bile duct (Figure 3). The bile duct also didn't show any sign of dilation or stenosis after the worm exit. But it was not possible to check if the bile duct had developed any complications later on as the patient didn't show up for a follow-up USG scan. The hematologic profile of the patient returned to normal values (the total bilirubin came down to 1.2 mg/dl and the direct bilirubin decreased to 0.2 mg/dl) after the worm exit. After three days of hospital stay, the patient showed complete recovery and was discharged with a prescription for oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and metronidazole for one week.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Soil-Transmitted Helminths
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: biliary ascariasis
